newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean police launch raids in Hanbo scandal.
newsitem.headline: South Korean police launch raids in Hanbo scandal.

text.p: South Korean police raided offices of the foundering Hanbo Group, and top bankers were barred from travelling in a loan scandal that has rocked President Kim Young-sam's government in an election year.
Kim cancelled a trip to Europe to focus on the biggest financial crisis of his term.
Share prices dived despite a desperate government bid to rescue the market, and the central bank continued to pump money into the banking system to prevent a credit crunch.

Hanbo's flagship, Hanbo Steel Co, sought court protection after piling up debts of $5.8 billion to build a new steel mill that many analysts regard as a white elephant. A second unit of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate also applied for court protection from creditors.

Meanwhile, the tycoon at the centre of the scandal, Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo who helped bankroll the corrupt administration of former president Roh Tae-woo, was rushed to hospital after complaining of high blood pressure.
Kim ordered a probe into loans to Hanbo after opposition allegations of government influence-peddling.

Police raided the homes of Chung and his four sons together with offices of Hanbo Steel and 15 affiliates. "Search warrants were issued to seize evidence for any financial irregularities," prosecutor Lee Chung-soo said.

The Justice Ministry slapped overseas travel bans on heads of Hanbo Steel's major creditor banks -- Korea First Bank, Cho Hung Bank, Korea Exchange Bank and Korea Development Bank -- along with 13 others.
This brings to 29 the number of people banned from leaving the country over Hanbo's loan scandal.
A presidential aide said Kim's planned visit to Hungary, Poland, Turkey and Italy in early March had been indefinitely postponed because of "domestic problems".
The Hanbo scandal has embarrassed Kim's government, still smarting from a humiliating climbdown over a new labour law it was forced to send back to parliament after four weeks of industrial strife.
Kim's single term expires after presidential elections in December, but he is believed to be trying to extend his power by installing a protege in office.
An outlawed union group said it was abandoning once-a-week strikes on Wednesdays, partly due to economic turmoil caused by the Hanbo collapse.
But the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said it still planned to go ahead with full stoppages starting on February 18 unless the government scrapped the law.
Hanbo has been embroiled in controversy ever since a multi-million dollar housing scandal involving its construction unit surfaced in 1991.

Chung paid 15 billion won into a slush fund raised by Roh, now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses. But a Seoul court trying Chung and Roh acquitted Chung on the grounds the money was forcibly extracted.
The ruling New Korea Party and opposition groups agreed to reopen parliament soon to debate the scandal.

Hanbo's woes again hammered the stock market, with banking and securities shares losing heavily. The index lost 1.85 points to 662.85, despite government attempts to boost sentiment by opening the door wider to foreign investment.
The central bank injected 600 billion won into the banking system after earlier providing three trillion won.
Financial analysts said the Hanbo debacle highlighted problems caused by industrial conglomerates obsessed with size over profits, but they said it could speed financial reform.

Chung is one of the leading patriachs of South Korea's family-run conglomerates that dominate the economy. Personal rivalry between chaebol heads has fuelled a drive by their companies into diverse business areas.
Banks have often been unwilling backers of reckless expansion, forced to extend loans by governments that have treated them as state cashiers.
